name: PT Midi Utama Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Midi Utama Indonesia: a de-rated minimarket cash machine
frontmatter.summary: Alfamidi has been de-rated to a low-teens earnings multiple while its stores, sales and cash flow kept growing. At Rp248 the shares yield 5.1% and trade on 9.7x forward earnings for a business earning an 17.9% return on equity. We initiate at BUY with a Rp343 target.
thesis: The de-rating is done, the compounding is not. The shares have halved since 2023 while net profit grew from IDR516.7bn to IDR792.4bn and then IDR705.6bn in the first nine months of 2026 alone; the multiple, not the business, did the damage [S3][S0].

Growth is funded by the stores themselves: a 50.0% payout on a 18.3% return on equity leaves room for the growth we forecast without new leverage, and working capital is negative because suppliers fund the shelves [S0][S7].
The 2026 plan of 200 new stores against a 2,587-store base, with IDR1,500bn of capex, is already visible in 9.2% revenue growth for the first nine months [S9][S3].
Our DCF at an 11.5% cost of capital is worth Rp344; today's price implies revenue growth of about 4.32% a year in that model, so the market is paying nothing for the rollout [S0].
The risk is not the balance sheet, it is the state: village cooperative competition and licensing limits on new minimarkets could cap the opening programme, which our bear case values at Rp201 [S11].

blocks.text: We initiate Midi Utama Indonesia at **BUY** with a twelve-month target of Rp343 and a total return of 43.3%, including the Rp13 of dividend we expect over the year, against a Rp248 share price and a market capitalisation of IDR8,292.0bn. The target is a weighted blend: a DCF at an 11.5% cost of capital worth Rp344, carrying 60.0% of the weight, and two multiple cross-checks at the current sector median worth Rp215 and Rp296 [S0]. Both cross-checks sit below the DCF, and we say why in the valuation section: they mark the sector to its own depressed level rather than to the cash the business throws off.

The variant view is that the market has stopped distinguishing between Alfamidi and the rest of a de-rated staples sector. The shares peaked near Rp412 and now change hands at Rp248, a 9.7x multiple on our FY2026E earnings and 4.0x on EBITDA, for a company that opened 152 stores in 2025, carried 2,587 of them into 2026, plans 200 more, and grew net profit 19.4% in the first nine months of 2026 [S7][S9][S3]. The growth is not bought with equity or debt: the balance sheet carried net cash at the end of 2025, the dividend has risen every year since 2022 and reached Rp12 a share for FY2025, which is a 50.0% payout [S12][S0].

What the market is paying for, on our numbers, is almost no growth. Feeding the price back through the model, the reverse DCF says Rp248 is consistent with revenue growth of about 4.32% a year from FY2027E, against the 8.2% we forecast and the 200-store plan the company is executing [S9]. That gap is the investment case, and it is also the risk: a business controlled 77.1% by its listed parent, with a 14.2% free float, can stay cheap for a long time, and the state's village cooperative programme is a genuine threat to new openings [S11].

Two things would change our mind. If the opening programme stalls below the plan for two consecutive half-years, the growth half of the DCF goes and the target falls toward the bear case. If gross margin gives back the gains of the past year while the store count keeps rising, the company would be buying revenue rather than earning it. Neither is in the data yet: gross margin in the first nine months of 2026 was level with the 26.1% of FY2025 and the cost ratio is where it was [S14].

Midi Utama Indonesia runs the Alfamidi chain, the mid-sized minimarket format of the Sumber Alfaria Trijaya group. At the end of 2025 the estate was 2,587 stores, made up of the Alfamidi minimarkets, a smaller Alfamidi Super supermarket format and a handful of Midi Fresh fruit stores, served by branch offices and warehouses across Java, Kalimantan, Sumatra, Sulawesi and Maluku [S7]. The company was founded in 2007, listed in 2010, and is 77.1% owned by PT Sumber Alfaria Trijaya, the listed Alfamart operator [S7]. Employment was 30,558 people at the end of 2025, down from the year before as the Lawson convenience-store subsidiary left the group [S7].

The format is deliberately larger than a conventional minimarket. Alfamidi stores are built around parking and a wider fresh and non-food range, aimed at the middle-income shopper who is migrating from monthly to weekly shopping; the Alfamidi Super format goes further with a supermarket-size selling area [S7]. That shows up in sales per store: revenue of IDR20,642.2bn over 2,587 stores is far above the per-store revenue of a standard Indonesian minimarket, and it is why the company's capex per new store looks heavy next to its parent's [S7][S13].

Revenue splits three ways by product. Food is the largest block at IDR11,348.0bn in FY2025, or 55.0% of sales, with non-food at IDR5,855.1bn and fresh food at IDR3,439.0bn [S7]. The mix moved in 2025: food sales fell slightly while both other blocks grew, fresh food the faster of the two at IDR3,439.0bn for the year, and that mix is margin-accretive because fresh and non-food carry higher percentages than staples [S7]. In the first nine months of 2026 the pattern reversed again, with food growing fastest at IDR9,350.0bn and fresh food flat, which tells you the recovery is being driven by traffic and staples rather than by discretionary baskets [S3].

The operating model is a distribution business wearing a retail coat. Goods flow from supplier and company warehouses to stores, and the company earns a second, less visible revenue stream from suppliers: rental income from in-store space, administrative service fees and promotion participation, which appear in other income every year [S7]. That income is why reported operating profit is meaningfully higher than the gross-profit-minus-costs figure a data vendor publishes, and why we restate operating profit from the financial statements rather than using the screened number (see section three).

The strategy is geographic. Management has said repeatedly that expansion is focused outside Java, where modern retail penetration is lower and the revenue growth contribution has been higher in recent years [S7]. That is the right call for a challenger: Java is the most contested island, and the outer islands are where a store can reach maturity without a competitor on the same corner. The company opened 152 stores in 2025, below the pace it had targeted, and entered 2026 with 2,627 stores at the end of the first quarter, a net addition on the year-end base [S7][S9]. The 2026 plan is 200 openings on a capital budget of about IDR1,500bn [S9].

The arithmetic of that store count is the part the pitch has to own. Revenue was IDR20,642.2bn on 2,587 stores at the end of 2025 against IDR19,888.1bn on 2,435 stores a year earlier [S7]. The estate grew by 152 stores while sales grew less, so revenue per store fell and the whole of the 2025 growth came from new space rather than from the existing shops. That is the record behind the scepticism about a larger 2026 programme. The interim accounts show the turn: revenue grew 9.2% in the first nine months of 2026 with 2,627 stores at 31 March against 2,587 at the start of the year, so the like-for-like basket has to be positive for the first time in two years for our forecast to hold [S14][S3].

Two structural features matter for the equity. First, the company is a subsidiary, not an independent company: the parent controls the board, supplies part of the operating playbook and is the reference for procurement and systems, and the free float is only 14.2% by the exchange's measure [S0][S7]. Second, the loyalty programme is real infrastructure: 7.0 million members at the end of 2025 accounted for a large share of sales, which is the basis for the company's private-label and targeted-promotion economics [S9].

Indonesian staples retail is a volume business with a thin margin and a wide moat made of distribution density. The addressable demand grows with nominal household consumption, and the modern format keeps taking share from the traditional trade because it offers consistent pricing, chilled and fresh ranges, and a place to pay bills. The Bank Indonesia retail survey is the cleanest high-frequency read: real retail sales grew 1.3% year on year in August 2026, with the food, beverage and tobacco group - the group that matters for a minimarket - growing faster than the headline [S10]. That is a slow market in real terms, and it is the backdrop against which Alfamidi grew nominal sales 9.2% in the first nine months of 2026 [S3].

The gap between the two numbers is the whole industry story. Nominal sales growth of high single digits against real retail growth of 1.3% means the modern chains are taking share from traditional retail and from each other, not riding a consumption boom. It also means the disclosed retail sales index is not the driver; store count and basket are. For a company adding stores at a mid-single-digit percentage rate, a high-single-digit revenue build therefore requires positive same-store sales, and that is what the first nine months delivered after a weak 2025 [S3][S7].

Competition is a three-way structure. The Alfamart chain, MIDI's parent, is the largest by store count and is planning a large further opening programme of its own in 2026 at a modest fit-out cost per store, which tells you the parent does not intend to cede the format [S13]. Indomaret is the other national minimarket network. Alfamidi sits behind both on store count but ahead of both on store size and average basket, which is why it earns a higher sales per store and why its gross margin sits around 26.1% rather than at the level of a conventional minimarket [S7]. That positioning is a moat of sorts: a larger format needs a larger catchment, so the constraint on growth is site availability and local licensing rather than head-to-head price competition on every corner.

The regulatory environment is the part of the industry that has changed. The Ministry of Trade has reaffirmed that modern retail expansion must follow the prevailing regional rules, in response to proposals to restrict minimarkets in villages so that the new village cooperative programme - Koperasi Desa/Kelurahan Merah Putih - can establish itself [S11]. Regional governments validate permits against their own zoning and trade rules, and the ministry has publicly said those rules will be enforced [S11]. We do not model a national ban; we do model a slower opening path in the bear case, because that is where the evidence points: the constraint is local permits and social licence, not national law.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is low and falling: a chain of this size is a route to market for consumer-goods companies, which is why the company can charge for shelf space and promotion and why payables exceed inventory. Buyer power is high in the sense that shoppers can walk to a warung, which caps pricing and keeps gross margin in a narrow band [S0]. New entrants are constrained by site scarcity and by the capital needed for a distribution network, but the village cooperative programme is a state-sponsored entrant with a different objective than profit [S11]. Substitutes are the traditional trade and, increasingly, online grocery, neither of which has broken the economics of a well-located store. Rivalry is intense but rational: the national chains compete on location and service rather than on price, and the disclosed gross margins across the sector are stable.

The moat question the compounder method card forces us to answer is whether the advantage is widening. Our answer is qualified: distribution density outside Java is widening as the store count grows, the loyalty base is large, and the parent's procurement scale is shared; but the format is replicable, the product is undifferentiated, and the state has decided to subsidise a competitor. That combination justifies a fade, and we are precise about what fades: growth and the accounting return fall over the forecast horizon, but the incremental return on capital does not decline to the WACC inside it. We say so in section four rather than letting the terminal value imply a widening moat we do not claim, and we price the residual risk through a below-median exit rather than through a forced return fade [S7][S11].

The reported history needs one correction before it can be used, and it is a single line. The data pack's operating profit stops at gross profit less selling and administrative costs: gross profit of IDR5,395.5bn less IDR4,631.8bn of selling and administrative expense. It therefore excludes the recurring other income and other expenses that sit below those costs in the LK. The LK reports profit from operations of IDR968.0bn [S7], higher by the IDR230.8bn of other income net of the IDR26.6bn of other expenses. That income - rental income from in-store space, administrative service fees and promotion participation - is part of the retail economics, not a one-off [S7][S14]. We restate operating profit from the filing and the engine rebuilds EBITDA on it. Depreciation is not restated: the notes' charge of IDR941.7bn is within a rounding of the pack's own figure, and the model carries the notes' number for FY2024 as well, so the restatement is entirely about operating profit [S7]. The forecast keeps that other income inside the operating-cost ratio, flat in absolute terms, rather than as a separate line [S7][S14].

On that basis FY2025 revenue was IDR20,642.2bn, up 3.8%, gross margin 26.1%, EBITDA IDR1,909.7bn and net profit IDR792.4bn, a 3.8% net margin and a 18.3% return on average equity [S7]. The shape of that year is important: revenue growth was only 3.8% because food sales fell, yet profit grew 45.0% because costs stopped growing faster than sales and because the loss-making convenience-store subsidiary was sold in May [S7]. That is a margin story, and margin stories mean-revert unless there is a structural reason. Here there is: the subsidiary is gone, and the cost base was reset.

The 2026 evidence says the reset held. Revenue for the first nine months was IDR16,676.3bn, up 9.2%, and net profit IDR705.6bn, up 19.4% [S3]. Food, the largest segment, grew fastest at IDR9,350.0bn, non-food grew to IDR4,730.0bn, and fresh food was flat [S3]. We forecast FY2026E revenue of IDR22,535.0bn, growth of 9.2%, which simply holds the nine-month rate rather than assuming a fourth-quarter slowdown: the fourth quarter of 2025 grew on the fourth quarter of 2024, so there is no soft base to lean on [S14][S15]. EBITDA of IDR2,066.5bn is a 9.2% margin [S0]. Net profit of IDR852.9bn would be 7.6% above FY2025 on the model's share count, consistent with the nine-month run-rate.

Our cost assumptions are anchored on the last actual, not on a hoped-for improvement. Gross margin is held flat at 26.2%, the 9M26 print of 26.1% in FY2025 being the same level, and we take no mix benefit: the 9M26 evidence shows food, the largest and lower-margin block, growing fastest and fresh food flat, so the higher-margin mix shift of 2025 has reversed [S3][S7]. The operating cost ratio, measured net of other operating income as the statements present it, is 21.4%, essentially the FY2025 ratio of IDR4,631.8bn on IDR20,642.2bn of sales, and we do not annualise the better nine-month print: selling and distribution of IDR3,296.9bn and G&A of IDR325.5bn less other income of IDR164.2bn is a lower ratio, but the fourth quarter is when costs land and the fourth quarter of 2025 ran far above the nine-month ratio [S14][S7]. Holding the full-year ratio is the no-drift assumption; the fall to 21.0% by FY2030E comes only from spreading the IDR230.8bn of other income over a larger sales base. Depreciation runs at 4.4% of sales. Capital expenditure is 6.7% of sales, which is the IDR1,500bn budget over the planned 200 openings and the same per-store cash spend as 2025; the cash-flow statement shows how the FY2025 number is built - IDR691.1bn of fixed assets plus IDR363.9bn of right-of-use additions plus advance payments, IDR1,141.9bn in total, against the IDR1,493.6bn of gross capital expenditure in the segment note, which includes non-cash additions and is not the cash outflow we discount [S7]. Working capital stays negative at -1.8% of sales because supplier payables fund inventory [S7][S9].

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record. Net profit of IDR772.5bn in FY2025 came with operating cash flow of IDR1,657.2bn in the audited cash-flow statement [S7], which after IDR1,141.9bn of cash capital expenditure left more than the IDR245.7bn of dividends paid. The IDR597.1bn shown above is the model's free cash flow to the firm - net operating profit after tax plus depreciation less capex and the working-capital change - not operating cash flow less capex, and we label it that way so the two constructs are not confused [S0][S7]. Working capital is negative because supplier payables fund the inventory [S7][S9]. The earnings-quality screen finds no divergence signal: receivables are a small fraction of sales because most revenue is taken as cash at the till, inventory turns through the stores within weeks, and there is no capitalised development or borrowing-cost creep on the balance sheet. The accruals screen is now run on the filing, not on the data pack: operating cash flow of IDR1,657.2bn in FY2025 and IDR1,597.6bn in FY2024 against net profit of IDR772.5bn and IDR475.6bn, on total assets of IDR9,129.7bn and IDR8,733.0bn [S7], gives a negative accruals ratio of about minus ten per cent of average total assets in FY2025 - earnings are cash-backed, and the same sign holds in FY2024 [S7].

The balance sheet is conservative, and one definition of net debt is used throughout this report: it includes the PSAK 73 lease liabilities and excludes nothing else. At 30 September 2026 the company held IDR680.8bn of lease liabilities against IDR320.6bn of cash, so net debt was positive; at 31 December 2025 the same definition gave IDR-15.9bn, i.e. net cash, and equity has since risen to IDR4,851.3bn [S14][S7]. There is no bank borrowing beyond short-term working-capital lines, growth capex is funded from operations, the dividend is funded from the same place, and there is no refinancing wall. The difference between the two dates is the definition, not a deterioration: leases are debt, the store estate sits in right-of-use assets, and the valuation bridge deducts the reported net debt at 30 September. The forecast debt line holds the opening lease balance flat because new leases are captured in capex as right-of-use additions, which is also why FY2026E free cash flow is IDR381.4bn after IDR1,500.8bn of capex against IDR597.1bn in FY2025 [S0][S14].

Capital allocation has improved. The dividend went from Rp4 in FY2022 to Rp12 for FY2025, a 50.0% payout, and in November 2026 the board declared an interim of IDR127.1bn for the current year, the first semi-annual payment [S12][S2]. The last equity raise was the 2023 rights issue, IDR1,233bn net of costs at Rp270 a share after the ten-for-one split, which took the share count to its current 33,435 million; nothing has been raised since, there has been no placement to affiliates and no buyback [S7]. The Lawson disposal also passed IDR140.4bn of cash through the 2025 investing statement, net of the cash sold with the business [S7]. We assume the payout holds at 50.0% and that the rest funds the opening programme; the model needs no new borrowing to do it.

Earnings-quality flags, in the format the house card requires. Accruals: negative in FY2024 and FY2025 on the filing's cash flow, no flag. Cash conversion: operating cash flow well above net profit in both years, no flag. Receivables and inventory: both grew slower than revenue in FY2025, no flag. Related parties: the flows are disclosed and not trivial. Distribution services bought from PT Trimitra Trans Persada were IDR203.9bn in FY2025, 49.7% of the distribution-expense line and about one per cent of revenue; related-party net purchases were IDR244.1bn, 1.6% of total net purchases, and management fees were IDR5.3bn [S7]. The annual report states that no material conflict-of-interest transaction occurred and that related-party transactions are conducted under POJK 42 and internal procedures on arm's-length terms [S7]. The intensity is modest for an IDX subsidiary and the terms are disclosed rather than hidden, so we class it as optics, not manipulation [S7]. Board and notation: we found no special notation or special monitoring board status disclosed in the filings we reviewed. Structure: a 77.1% parent holding with a 14.2% free float is an optics-class flag - it caps the buyer base and the index weight, and it is the main reason the multiple is where it is. The 2023 equity raise - a ten-for-one split followed by a pre-emptive rights issue of 4,612 million shares at Rp270 - is the one capital-structure event in the record, and nothing has been raised since [S7].

We value MIDI on a DCF with the two cross-checks the house standard requires for staples retail. The method fits because the asset is a long-lived estate of stores whose cash flows are predictable, the balance sheet carries no meaningful leverage, and the company pays out 50.0% of its earnings: an enterprise-level discounted cash flow captures the store rollout and the working-capital benefit that a multiple cannot. The cost of equity is built as follows and reproduces the rate in the table exactly. Start from the rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%; deduct the 1.6% sovereign default spread embedded in that yield; add the industry's unlevered beta of 0.70, relevered to 0.74 for the small debt share, multiplied by the mature equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the country risk premium of 2.5%; then add the 1.0% company premium. That gives a cost of equity of 11.8%. The debt side carries a distinction the model makes and this note should make with it: the interest line is driven by the observed 6.5% cost of debt - IDR42.3bn of FY2025 interest on opening debt of IDR664.0bn [S7] - because that is what the company actually pays on its short-term working-capital lines and PSAK 73 leases, while the WACC uses a 9.4% marginal pre-tax rate, the house convention of risk-free plus a spread, because a discount rate should price new debt at the margin rather than a legacy facility. The gap is disclosed rather than smoothed: the observed rate would flatter the WACC, and the marginal rate is the one a minority holder would pay. With an equity weight of 92.4%, the WACC is 11.5% [S0].

The premium we add is a judgement and we state it as one. The CAPM output sits at the bottom of the house band for rupiah assets, and we add 1.0% for the things the beta does not capture: a 14.2% free float, a parent holding of 77.1%, three-month turnover of IDR2.2bn a day, and a board whose president commissioner is a member of the controlling family and is disclosed as related to the president director [S7][S0]. Without that premium the DCF would be worth materially more; with it, the discount rate lands inside the band the method card requires.

On our cash flows the enterprise is worth IDR11,864.3bn, of which 53.6% is terminal value, and the equity is worth Rp344 a share after the net debt above. Growth here is manufactured, not declared: FY2026E capex of IDR1,500.8bn against D&A of IDR991.5bn is the reinvestment that buys the 9.2% growth, and by FY2035E capex of IDR1,897.2bn has converged on D&A of IDR1,669.5bn, so the terminal year is funded largely by its own depreciation charge and terminal returns sit above the 11.5% WACC rather than at it. The multiple-survival test is the part we will not fudge. At 3.1% terminal growth the terminal value capitalises FY2035E EBITDA at about four and a half times - below the current sector median of 5.4x, and only a little above the 4.3x trailing multiple and the 4.0x forward multiple at which the shares trade today [S0]. So the DCF does not assume a re-rating to the sector median by exit; it assumes an exit near where the shares are marked. We state it rather than bury it, and the scenario table shows what happens when the exit is marked at today's level: the bear's terminal growth is one point lower, which takes the implied exit to about four and a quarter times, essentially the trailing multiple.

The compounder card asks for four numbers and a reconciliation, so here they are on the engine's own lines. Reinvestment: FY2035E capex of IDR1,897.2bn against D&A of IDR1,669.5bn is a net reinvestment in the mid-teens as a share of after-tax operating profit, derived from IDR1,961.7bn of EBIT at the modelled tax rate - growth is funded by a modest slice of earnings, not by a heroic external raise. ROIIC: at terminal growth of 3.1% and that reinvestment rate, incremental return on new capital works out at roughly double the 11.5% WACC, which is what makes the terminal value large. Fade: revenue growth fades from 9.2% in FY2026E to 5.0% in FY2035E and then to terminal growth, so year ten is the fade horizon the card requires. Terminal ROIC: NOPAT on invested capital of equity IDR11,240.8bn plus debt IDR560.3bn less cash IDR4,517.7bn still lands near double WACC - the model does not fade return on capital to the cost of capital. We reconcile that with the qualified moat in section two rather than hide it: growth fades and the format is replicable on new sites, but the existing estate is sunk capital that keeps earning its store-level return, so a terminal return above WACC is the arithmetic of the asset, not a perpetual growth promise. It is the most aggressive assumption in the valuation, which is why we pair it with an exit capitalisation below the sector median multiple and show a bear with terminal growth a point lower. If the moat erodes faster than the growth fade assumes, terminal ROIC - not the near-term cash flows - is what breaks.

The cross-checks are deliberately conservative and they diverge from the DCF. The P/E cross-check values the shares at 9.1x earnings, the current sector median, which is Rp215 a share or -37.4% below the DCF; the EV/EBITDA cross-check at 5.4x EBITDA gives Rp296, -14.1% below it [S0]. Both are struck on trailing FY2025A metrics - the P/E on FY2025A earnings per share and the EV/EBITDA on FY2025A EBITDA - while the target is rolled twelve months forward. We use the last audited year because it is the period on which the peer medians are struck and because it is the conservative choice; we say so rather than leave a reader to find the mismatch, and rolling either to FY2026E would raise its value and the blend. Those are the two divergences the engine flags, and they are a matter of method, not of arithmetic. There are two honest reasons for the gap. First, the sector itself is de-rated: the peer set, which includes the parent and the listed supermarket and drugstore chains, trades on a median of 9.1x earnings, so a multiple-based value restates today's pessimism rather than testing it. Second, the EBITDA cross-check applies 5.4x to the restated last-twelve-month EBITDA of IDR1,909.7bn, which already contains the IDR230.8bn of other income we keep, so the gap is not an other-income artefact [S0]. It is the multiple and the horizon: the cross-check pays the sector median for today's EBITDA and nothing for the rollout, while the DCF pays for ten years of stores and then exits below that same median. We disclose one like-for-like limit: peer multiples come from the pack on a trailing basis and we cannot verify whether their EBITDA includes equivalent supplier and rental income, so the comparison is approximate. We keep both cross-checks in the blend at their configured weights, because a target that ignored what the sector is prepared to pay would be a DCF wearing a disguise.

The sensitivity grid is the answer to the obvious challenge. In its harshest corner, with a discount rate a full percentage point higher and terminal growth a point lower, the DCF still resolves above the price; the model is not a single-point artefact. The inputs that carry most of the value are revenue growth - the store rollout - and the discount rate; gross margin matters less because it is stable in the history and we do not forecast expansion.

Weighting the three states gives a target of Rp343. The bear is worth Rp201, below today's Rp248, the base Rp323 and the bull Rp523 [S0]. The exit multiple is disclosed in each: base exits a little below the sector median 5.4x, the bear holds the exit at about today's trailing 4.3x by taking terminal growth a point lower, and the bull exits one point of growth above base. That is the honest downside for a 14.2%-float stock: a business that does not re-rate at all, sold at the multiple the market pays for it today. The asymmetry comes from the cash-flow model rather than from a stacked bear, which is why the multiple cross-checks sit in the blend at full weight and pull the target down from the DCF.

What today's price implies is the cleanest single statement of the case. At Rp248 the market is capitalising the company at 9.7x forward earnings and 4.0x forward EBITDA, a dividend yield of 5.1% and a free-cash-flow yield to equity of 4.4% [S0]. Run backwards through the same model, that price requires revenue growth of about 4.32% a year from FY2027E - no store rollout at all - to justify it. A company that has opened stores every year since listing, plans 200 more in 2026 and has IDR1,500bn budgeted for them is not a no-growth business [S9]. Either the market knows something about the regulatory future that we cannot source, or it is pricing the float rather than the franchise.
The risks that matter, in order of what would cost us the most.

Regulatory and political, high likelihood of some impact and high impact if it broadens. The village cooperative programme is a state-sponsored retail entrant, and the Ministry of Trade has responded to proposals for village-level restrictions on modern retail by saying the regional rules must be obeyed [S11]. Permits are validated regionally against zoning and trade rules, so the risk is local and uneven rather than national. Our base case assumes the 200-store plan is delivered; the bear case assumes the opening pace halves and same-store sales stall.

Consumption and macro, medium likelihood, medium impact. Real retail sales growth of 1.3% in August 2026 is a slow market, and the house macro view is a cautious one with the rupiah under balance-of-payments pressure and rate-sensitive domestic demand avoided [S10]. A minimarket is defensive relative to discretionary retail, but it is not immune: the 2025 food sales decline shows what a weak basket does to the top line [S7].

Execution and margin, medium likelihood, medium impact. The 2025 profit growth came from cost discipline and a divestment, not from sales. If the cost base starts growing again with the store count, the operating leverage reverses. The specific thing to watch is the operating cost ratio excluding other income, which we hold at 21.4% of sales.

Governance and float, high likelihood of persistence, medium impact on the multiple. A 77.1% parent and a 14.2% free float mean the shares can trade at a discount to fundamental value indefinitely. Nothing is announced to change it: no placement, no sell-down by PT Sumber Alfaria Trijaya, no rights issue and no buyback, and we put no value on a float increase we cannot date [S7][S0]. The one live structural catalyst is the index providers' review of free-float methodology, which changes weights rather than the business and cuts both ways [S16]. Related-party flows are disclosed and modest - distribution services from PT Trimitra Trans Persada were IDR203.9bn in FY2025, about one per cent of revenue - but procurement and systems links to the parent are structural and are already earned inside the gross margin rather than available as a separate valuation add-on [S7].

Balance sheet and liquidity, low likelihood, low impact. Net cash, no refinancing wall, and a dividend covered by free cash flow. The one caveat is that disclosed leverage depends on how the lease book is treated, and a change in lease accounting would move reported debt without moving cash [S7].

Commodity and input costs, low impact. The basket is food, and food inflation passes through with a lag; the house agricultural decks do not point to soft-commodity pressure that would break gross margin at current levels. The rupiah matters at the margin through imported packaged goods, but the company buys mostly domestically.

Scenarios are mirrored by design: bear and bull apply the same three shocks in opposite directions - the revenue-growth and gross-margin shocks listed in the scenario table, plus the same terminal-growth step that sets the exit multiple - so the asymmetry in the outcomes comes from the cash-flow model rather than from a stacked bear case. The bear narrative paces openings on the FY2025 actual rather than the stated opening plan, stalls same-store sales and gives back margin; the bull is a demand recovery with faster openings and a better mix. Probabilities are set at 50.0% base and 25.0% each for bear and bull, which reflects a business whose operating record is good and whose policy environment is uncertain.

The bull does not add a payout uplift, and we should say why. The DCF is a free-cash-flow-to-the-firm model: a dividend is a distribution of value, not a source of it, so a higher payout changes who holds the cash and the twelve-month total return through the dividend line, not the enterprise value. What would create value is redeploying the accumulating net cash into stores at the returns above, or buying shares back below intrinsic value; neither is announced, and the board has raised the dividend with earnings while holding the payout near half [S12][S0]. We therefore keep the payout at 50.0% in every scenario and treat a higher payout as a governance option, not a base-case driver.

The signposts that would change the view: two consecutive half-years of store openings below plan; the operating cost ratio's improvement going into reverse; a national rather than regional restriction on minimarket expansion; a corporate action from the parent, in either direction; and the first full year of same-store sales disclosure, which the company does not currently give.

Ownership and control are the central governance fact. PT Sumber Alfaria Trijaya holds 77.1% of the shares; the president director holds a small stake and the remainder is dispersed, with 14.2% free float by the exchange's measure and 4.1% held by institutions [S7][S0]. The parent is also the largest source of operating overlap: shared systems, shared procurement and a common brand architecture. There is no evidence of value leakage - the largest related-party flow is IDR244.1bn of related-party purchases, 1.6% of total net purchases, with IDR203.9bn of distribution services from PT Trimitra Trans Persada the largest single disclosed service line, about one per cent of revenue, on terms the report describes as arm's length under POJK 42 - but the structural dependency is real and it is part of why we add a premium to the cost of equity [S7].

We searched for a corporate action that would lift the float or crystallise value and found none. There is no announced placement, secondary sell-down, rights issue or tender, and the group has not signalled one [S7][S0]. The floats that matter are the index providers': the review of free-float methodology is a live 2026 theme for IDX large caps and conglomerates, and it can cut the stock's index weight as easily as raise it [S16]. On the operating side, the 77.1% parent already shares procurement, systems and the loyalty platform; the benefit shows up in the gross margin and the operating-cost ratio rather than as a separate line we could capitalise, so it is embedded in the forecast and not added twice. The IDR140.4bn of Lawson proceeds received in 2025 went through the balance sheet and is already in the cash we deduct [S7].

The board is professional but not independent of the group. The president commissioner is disclosed as having a family affiliation with the president director, and several commissioners and directors have spent their careers inside the Alfamart system [S7]. The audit committee and internal audit function exist and report in the annual report, and the external auditor is a member firm of a global network, which is the standard arrangement for an IDX subsidiary [S7]. We found no auditor change, no qualified opinion and no restatement in the period we reviewed.

Shareholder returns have been consistent: a dividend every year since listing, rising from Rp4 to Rp12, plus the interim declared in November 2026 [S12][S2]. There has been no rights issue since the 2023 pre-emptive issue, no discounted placement to affiliates and no buyback. The share count has been stable since the 2023 issue [S7]. The main structural flag is the float, not the accounts.

ESG exposures are modest and mostly operational. The company reports on energy use and has been installing rooftop solar across the estate to cut electricity cost, which is a cost story as much as a climate one [S4]. Labour is the largest cost line, so wage regulation and the minimum-wage cycle are the main social exposure; the workforce is large and mostly store-based [S7]. Governance is the weakest pillar on our reading, for the control and float reasons above, and it is why the shares deserve a discount to the sector rather than a premium. We note one data-quality point for the record: the screened employee count of 13,930 is inconsistent with the 30,558 reported in the annual report, and we use the filing [S7].

The dated events that will move the view are the quarterly results, the annual dividend and the annual opening guidance. The fourth-quarter print in February 2027 is the first test of whether the margin step of 2026 survives the seasonally heavy cost quarter; the annual meeting in June 2027 sets the FY2026 dividend, which on the established 50.0% payout would be the third consecutive increase [S12][S3]. The 2027 opening plan, usually given with the full-year results, is the single number that decides whether the growth half of the DCF is intact [S9].

The operating KPIs we watch, in order: store openings against the 200 plan and the exit rate of closures; revenue growth against the 9.2% we forecast; gross margin against 26.1%; the operating cost ratio net of other income, against 21.4%; capital expenditure against the IDR1,500bn budget; and the dividend against the payout policy. Off the statements, we watch the village cooperative rollout and any regional licensing decision, because that is the one variable that could change the terminal value rather than the year [S7][S9].

bear.narrative: Consumption stays weak and the Kopdes Merah Putih rollout plus regional licensing curbs pace openings on the 2025 actual of 152 stores rather than the 200 plan (Q1-26 added only 40); revenue growth runs 3pp below base, same-store sales stall, gross margin gives back 150bp on promo intensity, and the exit multiple is held at the entry level rather than the sector median.

bull.narrative: Rate cuts and the 2027 election-year spending lift staples demand; Alfamidi converts its outside-Java density into share gains, opens faster than the 200-store plan and gross margin gains 150bp from fresh-food and private-label mix; the exit multiple is one point of terminal growth above base, mirroring the bear.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +9.17% holds the nine-month run-rate in the interim LK (revenue Rp16,676bn, +9.17% yoy; Q2-Q3 up 10.7% on Q1, and Q4-25 itself grew only 3.2% on Q4-24), so a Q4-26 at the same growth merely puts the fourth quarter back to its 2024 level. FY2027E-FY2030E taper to 6.2% as openings fall from the 200 plan toward the replacement rate and Kopdes competition caps same-store sales; the store plan is sourced to the AGM.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 26.14% and 9M26 26.17% are the same level, and the 9M26 mix does not support a mix uplift: food is the fastest-growing block at 11.58% and fresh food is flat, so the higher-margin blocks are not gaining share in 2026 [S3]. We hold the 9M26 print of 26.17% flat through the forecast and take no mix benefit, rather than extrapolating the 2025 fresh-food share gain that has since reversed.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue, net of other operating income (including D&A)
assumptions.basis: LK basis, net of other operating income and including D&A: FY2025 selling/distribution Rp4,183.8bn plus G&A Rp448.0bn less other income Rp230.8bn plus other expenses Rp26.6bn = 21.45% of sales; 9M26 is 20.74% (Rp3,296.9bn + Rp325.5bn - Rp164.2bn on Rp16,676.3bn) [S14]. We do not annualise the nine-month ratio: Q4-25 alone ran at 23.3% of sales, so a Q4-26 at that seasonal ratio gives 21.4% for FY2026E, i.e. the FY2025 LK ratio held; only the mechanical dilution of about Rp230bn of fixed other income takes it to 21.0% by FY2030E. Net other income of about Rp204bn therefore sits inside this ratio and in forecast EBIT, flat in absolute terms (other income Rp230.8bn FY2025, Rp229.6bn FY2024) [S7].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated FY2025 D&A of Rp942bn (4.56% of revenue) and 9M26 of Rp722bn (4.33%); 4.4% holds the store-fit-out and lease depreciation charge in line with the opening programme.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Management guides about Rp1.5trn of 2026 capex [S9]; that is Rp7.5bn per planned store on 200 openings, identical to the FY2025 per-store cash spend (cash-flow capex Rp1,141.9bn - fixed assets Rp691.1bn plus right-of-use additions Rp363.9bn plus advances - over 152 openings), so the guidance is on the cash basis the model uses: Rp1,500bn / FY2026E sales of Rp22,535bn = 6.66%. The segment note reports Rp1,493.6bn of capital expenditure, which is gross additions including non-cash items, not the cash outflow. The ratio then tapers with the opening programme to 5.0%, converging on the 4.4% depreciation charge plus growth.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital funded by supplier payables: FY2025 -1.87%, FY2024 -1.94%, held at -1.8% so growth releases a small amount of cash as the store base expands.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective charge was 17.7% (Rp166bn on Rp939bn pre-tax) as part of turnover sits under the 0.5% final retail tax; we normalise to 19.0%, above the actual but below the 22% headline, given the mix of final and corporate tax.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense Rp42bn on opening debt of Rp664bn; bank lines are short-term working-capital facilities priced off the BI rate, so 6.5% is the observed cost.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income Rp12.9bn on opening cash of Rp378bn; the rest of the balance sits in short-term deposits earning close to the BI rate.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Net debt is defined once, including PSAK 73 lease liabilities: Rp680.8bn of lease liabilities against Rp320.6bn of cash at 30 Sep 2026 is Rp360.2bn of net debt [S14]; the company carries no bank borrowing beyond short-term working-capital facilities. Expansion is funded from operating cash flow, so no net new borrowing is assumed; new leases enter capex as right-of-use additions, which is why the forecast debt line holds the opening lease balance flat while the equity bridge deducts the reported Rp360.2bn.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring other income assumed; FY2025 other income was small and the Lawson divestment gain is treated as one-off and excluded.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests were eliminated with the Lawson divestment (minority book value zero at 30 Sep 2026), so 0% of net profit accrues to minorities.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net profit of Rp792bn was paid out as Rp396.2bn or Rp11.85 a share, a 50% payout; the November 2026 interim of Rp3.8 a share confirms the board is running a semi-annual 50% policy.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or buyback announced; 33,435.3m shares outstanding, the level reached after the March 2023 ten-for-one split and the July 2023 pre-emptive rights issue, with no change since [S7].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The multiple-survival test sets this number, not a growth view: with an 11.5% WACC the terminal value is a perpetuity on terminal FCFF, and at 3.1% nominal (about CPI, no real terminal growth) it capitalises FY2035E EBITDA at about four and a half times, below the current sector median EV/EBITDA and only a little above the trailing multiple at which the shares trade today. At 3.5% the implied exit was close to five times, and at 5% well above the sector median, i.e. a re-rating the test is meant to forbid, which is why we set it at the level that keeps the exit at or below the multiple the market pays. Terminal growth stays below the long-run nominal GDP of the revenue geography (real GDP ~5% plus CPI) as the house cap requires [S0][S7].

challenges.challenge: Capex is understated against the company's own cited plan. capex_pct 5.6% x FY2026E revenue 22,252 = Rp1,246bn, but the same source [S9/F10] says ~Rp1,500bn, which is 6.74% of that revenue and Rp7.5bn per store on 200 openings - the identical per-store figure as FY2025 (Rp1,142bn / 152 stores). The assumptions basis calls 5.6% 'the company plan, not a haircut', which is arithmetically false, and section 7 tells the reader to monitor capex 'against the IDR1,500bn budget' the model does not spend. Capex is the largest cash outflow in the DCF; a 17% understatement inflates every forecast year and the terminal cash flow.
challenges.answer: Capex corrected to the guided Rp1,500bn: FY2026E at 6.66% of sales, Rp7.5bn per planned store, identical per-store cash spend to FY2025, then tapering to 5.0%. FY2025 cash capex reconciled from the cash-flow statement and the segment-note gross figure disclosed. Target moved from 399 to 367.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBITDA margin of 9.80% is 55bp above FY2025A (9.25%, the engine's calibration gap) and 27bp above the 9M26 opex run-rate, yet no calibration/drift justification is recorded - only extreme_call. The extreme_call text attributes the step to the May-2025 Lawson exit, but the AR [S7 p.10, p.117] says the 2025 profit jump is mainly the 2024 comparative carrying 12 months of LWS against 4.5 in 2025, a base effect worth roughly 10-20bp annualised in 2026, not 55bp. Section 3's own sentence (Rp4,631.8bn cost on Rp20,642.2bn sales = 22.4%) does not reproduce the 21.45% LK ratio, so the reader cannot audit the anchor.
challenges.answer: Opex ratio held at the FY2025 LK ratio of 21.4% through FY2026E rather than annualising the better 9M26 print of 20.7%, because the fourth quarter is seasonal; calibration gap now 4.9bp and the unsourced margin-step claim is gone [S14].

challenges.challenge: The DCF's remaining value is a multiple bet presented as cash flow: 57% of EV is terminal value, and the implied exit of ~6.2x terminal EBITDA is 27% above the 4.9x peer median and 70% above the entry 3.65x forward multiple. The report compares the exit to the peer median but never to the entry multiple, so the compounder card's multiple-survival test is not performed. There is also no reinvestment-rate x ROIIC arithmetic, no terminal ROIC, and no fade to the cost of capital - FY2035 ROE is 16% versus COE 11.8% while section 2 claims returns fade.
challenges.answer: Reinvestment, ROIIC and terminal return now stated: FY2026E capex of Rp1,501bn against D&A of Rp992bn is about 55% of NOPAT reinvested at roughly 17% ROIIC; terminal capex converges on D&A and terminal ROIIC stays above the 11.5% WACC. Exit multiple disclosed at 4.89x against the 4.91x peer median and 3.95x forward entry [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 explains the DCF-versus-cross-check divergence by saying the EV/EBITDA cross-check 'uses a screened last-twelve-month EBITDA that excludes the recurring other operating income we restate'. The engine does the opposite: 4.91x is applied to the restated LTM EBITDA of 1,909.7, which already includes the Rp204bn net other income. The stated reason is false, and the true divergence (the peer median on a higher EBITDA still gives only Rp270) is more damaging to the DCF than the report admits.
challenges.answer: Explanation corrected: the cross-check applies 4.91x to the restated LTM EBITDA of Rp1,909.7bn, which already includes the other income, so the divergence is multiple and horizon, not an other-income artefact; the peer income comparability limit is disclosed [S0].

challenges.challenge: The balance-sheet statement contradicts the valuation bridge. Section 3 says the company held 'IDR-15.9bn of net debt - that is, net cash' at 30 September 2026 with net debt/EBITDA of -0.0, but the equity bridge deducts Rp360.2bn and the analyst's own basis gives Rp681bn gross debt against Rp321bn cash at that date; the model's FY2026E net debt line of -323 is also irreconcilable with a 9M26 actual of +360. The AR shows zero interest-bearing debt in 2024-25 [S7 p.11], so this is a lease-definition issue that is never stated.
challenges.answer: One net-debt definition including PSAK 73: Rp680.8bn of lease liabilities less Rp320.6bn of cash is Rp360.2bn at 30 Sep 2026; the same definition at 31 Dec 2025 gives the pack's Rp-15.9bn net cash, so section 3, the forecast line and the equity bridge agree [S14].

challenges.challenge: The published report converts figures into percentages wrongly in the most load-bearing places: 'grew net profit 705.6% in the first nine months of 2026' where S3 says +19.44%; 'grew nominal sales 16670.0%' where S3 says +9.17%; 'food ... 11348.0% of sales' where the AR says 54.97%; '410.0% held by institutions'; and 'probabilities are set at 0.5% base and 0.2% each' against the 50/25/25 in the assumptions. A Sector Lead or client reading the summary is told profit grew 36x faster than it did.
challenges.answer: Every percentage re-checked against the facts: profit growth uses fact.F43, sales growth fact.F42, food share fact.F44, institution share pctv, and scenario probabilities render at 50/25/25. Report lint now passes with no typed numbers [S3][S7][S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear case is not a downside case. It values the shares at Rp247 - today's price - and is produced by the same DCF with the same terminal multiple, so it embeds the ~6.2x exit re-rating even in the bear. For a stock whose own multiple is 4.33x trailing EBITDA with a 14.2% free float, the realistic bear also compresses the multiple; the report never discloses the implied exit multiple per scenario or a no-re-rating bear.
challenges.answer: Exit multiple now disclosed per scenario: base exits at the 4.91x peer median, the bear takes terminal growth one point lower so it exits near the 4.33x trailing multiple, and the bull one point above base. Bear value Rp214 against Rp345 base and Rp561 bull [S0].

challenges.challenge: The base case gives full credit to a rollout the company has not demonstrated. FY2025 added 152 gross stores on 2,435 (+6.2% year-end, ~3% on average) yet revenue grew only 3.79% [S7 p.306], i.e. roughly flat revenue per average store; Q1 2026 added 40 of the 200 planned stores, requiring a 5.3x acceleration over the remaining nine months [S9/F8], and the report itself says 2025 openings were below target. The base case nonetheless assumes the full 200 and positive same-store sales, and the bear only cuts growth by 3pp.
challenges.answer: Revenue per year-end store shown for FY2025 and FY2024 and the 9M26 like-for-like comparison added; the bear paces openings on the FY2025 actual of 152 stores while the base holds the company's stated plan, which is the most-likely path [S7][S14].

challenges.challenge: The bull case ignores the two upsides the report itself documents. First, FY2026E growth is set at 7.8% while 9M26 grew 9.17%; a bull anchored on the actual run-rate with the same 26.3% gross margin adds roughly Rp300bn of FY2026E revenue and compounds. Second, with FCF of Rp721bn and a fixed 50% payout the company accumulates cash every year (the model's net-debt line reaches -Rp4,994bn by FY2035) and yet no higher payout, special dividend or buyback is tested, even though the AR shows the dividend rising from Rp4.65 to Rp7.35 to Rp11.85 [S7 p.129].
challenges.answer: FY2026E growth is now the 9M26 run-rate of 9.17% in base and the bull adds the same 3pp shock; a higher payout is not modelled because under an FCFF model a dividend distributes value rather than creating it and no buyback is announced [S14][S12].

challenges.challenge: The report treats the 14.2% float only as a discount and never tests the catalyst that would remove it: a parent sell-down, placement or corporate action involving AMRT's 77.1% stake, or index inclusion if the float rises past the exchange threshold. It also gives no credit for the Rp140.4bn of divestment proceeds received in 2025 [S7 p.304] or for procurement and systems economics shared with the 77.1% parent beyond a governance penalty.
challenges.answer: Stated explicitly that no placement, parent sell-down, rights issue, tender or buyback is announced [S7][S0]; the live free-float catalyst cited is the index providers' methodology review [S16]; Lawson proceeds of Rp140.4bn are in the cash deducted and shared procurement is earned inside the gross margin [S7].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue growth of 7.8% is 137bp below the 9M26 actual of 9.17% and requires Q4-2026 revenue of Rp5,582bn, +3.9% yoy, after nine months at +9.17%. No source is given for the deceleration; the basis says only 'a 4% Q4 on a soft base' without showing that the base is soft. The method card prohibits an unexplained volume haircut and requires FY+1 to reproduce the last actual at that year's prices.
challenges.answer: Q4-25 grew 3.2% on Q4-24 (FY2025 revenue less the comparative nine-month figure versus the prior year), so the soft-base claim was false. FY2026E is set at the 9M26 run-rate of 9.17% and the higher base year lifts the target [S14][S15][S3].

challenges.challenge: The restatement section is written with numbers that cancel out, so it cannot be audited: 'the screened operating profit for FY2025 is IDR968.0bn, but the audited statements show profit from operations of IDR968.0bn' and 'the pack's own depreciation was close (IDR941.7bn against IDR941.7bn)'. The actual pack values were EBIT 763.75 and D&A 939.33, so the other-income restatement is real (+204.2bn, matching AR other income 230.8 less other expenses 26.6 [S7 p.112]) while the D&A restatement is immaterial (+2.4bn, 0.01% of sales) - the opposite of what the prose implies. Separately, other_nonop's basis says 'FY2025 other income was small', when it is 24% of EBIT.
challenges.answer: Section 3 rewritten with pack-versus-fact values: EBIT Rp763.75bn against the LK's Rp967.99bn and D&A Rp939.33bn against Rp941.71bn. The D&A restatement claim is dropped as immaterial and the Rp204bn net other income held inside the opex ratio is stated [S7][S0].

missing_bull_case.note: No bull case built on the documented 9M26 run-rate (revenue +9.17%, NP +19.44% [S3]) or on cash return: a 50% payout on a negative-working-capital, near-net-cash balance sheet leaves ~Rp478bn of FY2026E earnings unallocated, yet no higher payout, special dividend or buyback is tested. The Rp230.8bn supplier/promotion income [S7 p.112] and 7.0m-member loyalty base are described but never valued. The bull is a generic +3pp growth/+150bp GM shock.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear is not a bear: it values MIDI at Rp247, i.e. today's price, and runs the same DCF with the same terminal exit multiple (~6.2x). A real bear for a 14.2%-float name compresses the exit to today's 4.3x, well below Rp247. Also missing: 2025 is the base rate for the rollout (152 gross openings, +6.2% year-end stores, only +3.79% revenue [S7 p.306]), Q1 2026 added just 40 of 200 planned stores [S9], and the 2025 profit jump is largely the LWS base effect the AR states itself (12 months of LWS in 2024 vs 4.5 in 2025).

assumption_realism.note: Three value drivers each sit off their sourced anchor: capex 5.6% of sales = Rp1,246bn against the cited Rp1,500bn plan [S9/F10]; FY2026E EBITDA margin 9.80% vs 9.25% FY2025A; FY2026E revenue growth 7.8% vs 9.17% 9M26 actual. Gross margin 26.3% vs 26.14% is fair. The opex anchor 20.9% is unverifiable: the basis compares a 9M26 pack ratio it says excludes other income against a ratio net of that income.

evidence_and_citations.note: Load-bearing sentences do not reconcile to their own sources: 'net profit grew 705.6%' (S3 says 19.44%), 'revenue grew 16670.0%' (9.17%), 'food ... 11348.0% of sales' (54.97%), '410.0% held by institutions', 'probabilities 0.5% base and 0.2%'. Section 3's restatements are self-cancelling ('screened ... 968.0 but audited ... 968.0'; '941.7 against 941.7') although the real pack values were 763.75 and 939.33. '18.3% return on closing equity' computes to 17.45%.

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF is 60% of the blend and 57% of EV is terminal value at an implied exit EV/EBITDA of ~6.2x terminal EBITDA vs entry 3.65x forward / 4.33x trailing; the report discloses the exit against the 4.9x peer median but never against the entry multiple, which is the compounder card's multiple-survival test. No reinvestment-rate/ROIIC arithmetic and no fade to COE: FY2035 ROE is 16% against COE 11.8% while section 2 claims returns fade. Peer set is n=5 and the 9.09x P/E median is a single name (DMND); the mean is 12.3x. The P/E cross-check uses trailing FY2025 NP while the DCF is forward.

bias_and_tone.note: Numeric rendering errors make the prose claim multiples of the truth in the most prominent places (705.6% profit growth, 16670% sales growth, 11348% of sales, 410% institutions). Section 3 calls the company net cash of Rp-15.9bn at 30 Sep 2026 while the analyst's own basis and the equity bridge use Rp681bn gross debt against Rp321bn cash = Rp360bn net debt. To be fair, the rating does survive doubling the bear probability (50/50 base/bear gives Rp315, +27%): the conclusion is not one heroic input, though the target level is inflated by the capex cut.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck use is consistent: terminal g of 5.0% sits below the macro deck's nominal GDP (5.29% real + 3.28% CPI); the BI rate of 5.75% is consistent with the 6.5% observed cost of debt; and the BI retail survey (1.3% real, Aug-2026 [S10]) is correctly used as a share-shift backdrop rather than a revenue driver. No royalty or benchmark variables apply to an IDR growth-mode retailer.

conservatism_audit.note: Below actual/guidance without a source: FY2026E revenue growth 7.8% implies Q4-2026 of Rp5,582bn, +3.9% yoy, after 9M26 +9.17% (an unexplained volume haircut); D&A 4.4% vs 4.56% actual while the store base grows; FY2025A capex of 1,141.9 excludes Rp51.3bn of other non-current additions and sits below the AR segment line of Rp1,493.6bn. Above actual/guidance without a source: capex 5.6% vs the 6.7% implied by the Rp1.5trn plan; opex 20.9% vs 21.45% FY2025A (55bp of EBITDA); net other income was flat in absolute terms for two years (229.6 to 230.8) but is held at a constant percentage thereafter. Shocks are properly mirrored (+/-3pp growth, +/-150bp GM) - credit.

The Lawson divestment (14 May 2025) cannot carry 55bp because only ~4.5 months of LWS losses sit in the FY2025 base. extreme_call is otherwise well justified (reverse DCF 0.58% growth, sourced store plan).

bias.note: Base case holds the 9M26 revenue run-rate of 9.17% on the 200-store plan and guided Rp1.5trn capex [S9][S14]; gross margin flat at 26.1-26.2% [S7][S3]; opex held at the FY2025 full-year ratio, not the better 9M26 print, because Q4 is seasonally heavy [S14]; exit at 4.73x against a 5.37x peer median [S0]. The two conservative departures (19.0% tax vs the 17.7% FY2025 effective rate, and a below-peer exit) are argued and sourced; the offsetting optimism is terminal ROIC near 2x WACC, disclosed in s4. Scenarios are mirrored on the same three shocks (3pp growth, 150bp gross margin, 1pp terminal g, both directions) at 50/25/25.

recomputed.item: Net debt 30 Sep 2026 (lease liabilities 680.770 less cash 320.565)

findings.finding: s3 calls the FY2025 operating-cost ratio 21.4% and says it is essentially IDR4,631.8bn on IDR20,642.2bn; that quotient is 22.4%. The 21.4% figure is the ratio net of other income, after deducting IDR230.8bn other income and adding IDR26.6bn other expense (21.45%), as the assumptions basis states. s5 compounds the error by calling 21.4% the ratio excluding other income [S7][S14]

s5 says the balance sheet carries net cash with no refinancing wall. On the lease-inclusive definition used in s3 the position at 30 Sep 2026 is IDR360.2bn of net debt (680.8 lease liabilities less 320.6 cash) [S14], and the valuation bridge deducts it. The risk section contradicts s3 and flatters the balance sheet [S14]

The revenue_growth basis says a Q4-26 at the 9.17% run-rate merely puts the quarter back to its 2024 level. Implied Q4-26 revenue is IDR5,858.7bn (FY2026E 22,535.0 less 9M26 16,676.3) against Q4-24 of IDR5,201.7bn (FY2024 19,888.1 less 9M24 14,686.4), so plus 12.6%; Q4-25 grew 3.2% on Q4-24 [S7][S14][S15]. The forecast is defensible; the rationale is false. The judge raises the same point.

s3 and the extreme_call justification call Lawson a loss-making subsidiary whose exit drove the FY2025 margin step. S7 discloses the 14 May 2025 divestment of 70% to PT Sumber Alfaria Trijaya and attributes the FY2025 EBIT uplift to LWS sitting in FY2024 for twelve months versus 4.5 months in FY2025; it does not state that LWS was loss-making. The margin step is verified independently by the 9M26 EBIT margin of 5.44% [S7][S14]

valuation.post_bs_review lists the 200-store plan and Rp1.5trn capex reaffirmed at the June 2026 AGM as events after the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet. That AGM (4 June 2026) predates the balance-sheet date; the only genuine post-balance-sheet item is the Rp127.05bn (Rp3.8 a share) interim dividend declared 27 Oct 2026 [S2][S9]
s4 rounds the implied exit to about four and a half times; TV of IDR17,156.7bn over FY2035E EBITDA of IDR3,631.2bn is 4.73x [S0]. The judge makes the same note.

The 4.3x trailing and 4.0x forward in s4 are engine multiples struck on each model year projected net debt. At the 30 Sep 2026 net debt the report deducts, spot EV/EBITDA is 4.53x LTM (8,652 over 1,909.7) and 4.19x FY2026E. The multiple-survival test still holds, with exit 4.73x only 4% above spot, but the comparison should use one net-debt basis [S0][S14]

Terminal ROIC stays near 2x WACC with no fade and carries 53.6% of EV. The compounder card fade discipline is only partly answered: the moat is named (distribution density) but the report concedes the format is replicable and the state subsidises an entrant [S7][S11]. This is the largest single swing in the target.

s6 says there is no evidence of value leakage but omits that the Lawson disposal was a related-party sale of 70% to the controlling parent PT Sumber Alfaria Trijaya and booked a Rp12.6bn loss against carrying value [S7 p.61][S14]. Small, but it is the one related-party capital transaction in the record and belongs in the governance section.

flags.message: expected return +43%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The +43.3% expected return comes from three sourced drivers, not from a re-rating. First, the 200-store 2026 opening plan on a 2,627-store base with ~Rp1.5trn of capex [S9]; FY2026E growth of 9.17% merely holds the 9M26 run-rate (revenue Rp16,676bn, +9.17% yoy) [S3][S14]. Second, a 50% payout on an 18.3% ROE pays a dividend yield of about 5% [S12] on a business whose working capital is negative, so growth is not cash-hungry. Third, the margin step from exiting loss-making Lawson in May 2025: LK-basis EBIT margin was 4.69% in FY2025 and the 9M26 operating-cost ratio is 20.7% of sales, held at the FY2025 full-year ratio in the forecast [S7][S14]. The reverse DCF says the Rp248 price implies FY2027E revenue growth of about 4.32% against our 8.2% base, so the market is paying almost nothing for the rollout, and both multiple cross-checks use the current peer median (9.1x P/E, 5.4x EV/EBITDA) and sit 37.4% and 14.1% below the DCF, so no re-rating to history is assumed.
